body:
Machines that act and devices that communicate

Modern technology allows machines to perform physical tasks, respond to their surroundings and exchange information. Three important concepts in this development are robotics, autonomous systems and the Internet of Things (IoT). They are related, but they do not mean the same thing.

Robotics concerns the development and use of machines that perform physical tasks under programmed control. A robotic arm can move an object from one location to another, while a mobile robot can travel through a warehouse. A robot commonly combines mechanical parts, a controller, actuators and, where required, sensors.

An autonomous system can perform specified tasks or make operational decisions without continuous human commands. Autonomy can be limited to a particular task or environment. For example, a robotic cleaner may independently move around a room but still require a person to empty its dust container. Autonomy does not mean unlimited intelligence or the complete absence of human supervision.

The Internet of Things connects physical or virtual things through communication technologies so that information can be collected, exchanged and used to provide services. A connected electricity meter can transmit consumption readings without physically moving like a robot.

How the concepts differ

ConceptMain characteristicSimple example
RoboticsProgrammed physical movement or manipulationIndustrial robotic arm
AutonomyCarrying out defined tasks without continuous human directionRobot adjusting its path around an obstacle
IoTNetworked exchange and use of information about thingsConnected electricity meter
Artificial intelligence (AI)Computational methods for tasks such as recognising patterns or making predictionsSoftware identifying objects in camera images

These concepts can overlap. A warehouse robot may use sensors to navigate, exchange its status with a central platform and employ AI to recognise objects. In that case, robotics, autonomous control, IoT connectivity and AI contribute different functions to the same system.

Robots are not necessarily humanoid

A humanoid robot resembles the human body in some aspects of its form or movement. However, most useful robots do not need a human-like appearance. Industrial manipulators, wheeled robots and specialised inspection robots may have entirely different structures.

The International Organization for Standardization, through ISO 8373:2021, describes robots in terms of programmed, actuated mechanisms with a degree of autonomy. It also distinguishes industrial robots, service robots and medical robots. In everyday language, remotely operated robotic devices are also commonly called robots, although a device with no autonomy may be distinguished from a robot under a strict technical definition.

Automation is not the same as autonomy. Automation means performing a process according to established instructions. Autonomy adds the ability to carry out defined tasks based on the current situation without requiring a human command for every action. Neither necessarily requires advanced AI or an Internet connection.

Prelims focus

  • A robot performs physical tasks through programmed mechanisms.
  • A sensor obtains information; an actuator produces an action.
  • IoT concerns connected things and information exchange, not necessarily physical movement.
  • A humanoid appearance is not required for a machine to be a robot.
  • ISO 8373:2021 is an international robotics vocabulary standard.
  • Trap: Every robot is not autonomous, AI-enabled or connected to the Internet.

[Sources: NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.2.4 and 2.4, reproduced by IIT Kanpur's SATHEE NCERT resource, accessed 2026-11-05; International Federation of Robotics, Industrial Robots and Service Robots, definitions based on ISO 8373:2021, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4218, section 3.1, May 2023, accessed 2026-11-05.]

title: Robotics, Autonomous Systems and the Internet of Things: Basic Concepts

body:
The main functional parts of a robot

A robot must be able to carry out an intended physical task. Many robots do this by collecting information, processing instructions and causing a mechanical movement. These functions are commonly described as sensing, control and actuation.

  • Sensors: Detect a physical condition, movement or other feature of the surroundings and convert it into information the controller can use.
  • Controller: Processes instructions and available sensor information to decide which action the robot should perform. It may be a microcontroller, computer or another programmed control unit.
  • Actuators: Convert a control command into a physical action, such as turning a wheel, moving a joint or opening a gripper.
  • Mechanical structure: Supports the robot and determines how its parts can move. It may include a frame, wheels, joints or an arm.
  • Power source: Supplies the energy needed for the controller, sensors and actuators. Depending on the robot, power may come from a battery or an external electrical supply.

What different sensors detect

A sensor responds to some property of the environment or the machine. A camera, for example, records images; a temperature sensor measures temperature. The sensor does not itself decide the robot's task.

SensorWhat it detectsTypical use
CameraLight and visual imagesRecognising objects or inspecting products
Ultrasonic sensorDistance using reflected high-frequency soundDetecting nearby obstacles
Infrared sensorInfrared radiation or reflected infrared light, depending on its typeProximity or temperature detection
LiDARDistance using reflected laser lightMeasuring surroundings for navigation
Wheel encoderWheel rotationEstimating movement of a wheeled robot
Accelerometer and gyroscopeAcceleration and rotational motionEstimating movement or orientation
Force or pressure sensorApplied force or pressureDetecting contact during handling

Different sensors may be combined because one sensor cannot measure every condition. For instance, a camera may identify an object, while a distance sensor estimates how far away it is. Neither reading guarantees perfect knowledge: measurements may be affected by the environment or by sensor limitations.

How actuators produce movement

An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical movement. It can turn a robot's wheels or move a joint through suitable mechanical arrangements. A gripper is a device fitted to a robot for holding an object; its opening and closing may be driven by an actuator.

The school-level foundation for motor-driven movement is the relationship between electricity and magnetism. Electric current produces a magnetic field, and electromagnetic forces can be used to create movement. The controller supplies the appropriate commands to the motor system; it does not itself provide the mechanical force.

Example: avoiding a wall

Consider a wheeled robot travelling towards a wall. A front-facing distance sensor detects that the obstacle is close. The controller compares the measured distance with a programmed condition and commands the motors to slow down, stop or turn. Subsequent sensor readings help the controller determine whether the obstacle has been avoided.

This example illustrates feedback: the robot uses information about the results of its movement to guide further actions. It also shows why sensing and actuation must be distinguished. Measuring the wall's distance is a sensing task; turning the wheels is an actuation task.

A sensor reports a condition, a controller selects or adjusts an action, and an actuator carries out the physical action. These functions may be combined within one machine, but they remain conceptually distinct.

Prelims focus

  • LiDAR uses laser light; ultrasonic ranging uses reflected sound.
  • Accelerometers detect acceleration; gyroscopes provide information about rotation.
  • Wheel encoders provide information about wheel rotation.
  • Motors are actuators, whereas cameras and thermometers are sensors.
  • Feedback uses observed conditions to adjust subsequent action.
  • Trap: A sensor does not automatically become an actuator merely because both are electronic devices.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 6, Electricity and Circuits, sections 12.3–12.4; NCERT, Curiosity, Class 6, Temperature and its Measurement, section 7.3; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Electric Current and its Effects, sections 14.3–14.5; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Control and Coordination, section 6.1, and Magnetic Effects of Electric Current, section 12.2, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volumes 28, 29 and 32; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, section 2.4.2, accessed 2026-11-05.]

title: How a Robot Works: Sensors, Controllers and Actuators

body:
Why control is necessary

A robotic machine must coordinate its movements so that it performs a task correctly. Its control system determines which movement should occur, when it should occur and, where sensors are available, whether the result is satisfactory.

The distinction between a fixed sequence and a response to changing conditions is especially important. A machine can repeatedly perform a task according to a program without independently understanding the surroundings.

Open-loop and closed-loop control

Open-loop control uses a prescribed command or sequence without measuring the result to correct that particular action. For example, a simple motor may be instructed to run for a fixed period. If an unexpected load slows the motor, the system may not compensate for it.

Closed-loop control uses feedback from sensors to compare an observed condition with the intended condition and make adjustments. For example, a robot may monitor its wheel rotation or position and alter motor operation when actual movement differs from the desired movement.

Closed-loop control is useful when conditions can change, but it does not guarantee safe or correct operation under every circumstance. Its performance still depends on suitable sensors, instructions and functioning equipment.

Who makes the operational decisions?

ModeWho directs the task?Example
Remote operationA human sends operating commands from a distanceRemotely controlled inspection device
Automatic operationA programmed system follows a defined processRobot arm repeating a handling cycle
Partly autonomous operationMachine handles some decisions; human supervises or intervenesRobot navigating a defined area with operator oversight
More autonomous operationMachine carries out a wider range of decisions within defined limitsMobile robot planning its route around detected obstacles

These modes are not always completely separate. A robotic system may work autonomously during normal conditions and switch to human control when it encounters an unfamiliar situation. The degree of autonomy must therefore be understood in relation to the particular task.

Is artificial intelligence necessary?

Artificial intelligence is not compulsory for robotics. A robot can use ordinary programmed rules, such as stopping when a measured distance falls below a chosen limit. More advanced systems may use AI to recognise objects, classify images or improve decisions based on data. Both types can be robotic systems.

Similarly, a robot does not require an Internet connection to carry out local control. A factory robot may continue following its programmed task even if it is not connected to a remote platform. Connection becomes useful when the machine must exchange operating information, receive authorised updates or coordinate with other systems.

Remote operation and autonomy must not be confused. A person controlling a machine from another location is still providing human control. Distance between the operator and the machine does not, by itself, make the machine autonomous.

Prelims focus

  • Open-loop control does not use the observed result to correct the action being performed.
  • Closed-loop control uses feedback to adjust an action.
  • Remote operation depends on human commands from a distance.
  • Autonomy means performing defined tasks without continuous human intervention.
  • Robotics can function without AI or Internet connectivity.
  • Trap: A machine following programmed instructions is not necessarily making independent decisions about unexpected conditions.

[Sources: International Federation of Robotics, Service Robots, explanation of degree of autonomy under ISO 8373:2021, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Control and Coordination, section 6.1, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volume 32; NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.2.4 and 2.4, accessed 2026-11-05.]

pictures.caption: Feedback distinguishes closed-loop control from a fixed open-loop command.

title: Robot Control, Automation and Degrees of Autonomy

body:
What navigation means

Navigation is the process of moving from one location to another while determining a suitable route. A mobile robot may need to know where it is, where it should go and whether its intended path is clear.

Navigation involves several related functions:

  • Position estimation or localisation: Estimating the robot's present location.
  • Mapping: Representing relevant features of the surrounding area, such as walls, paths or obstacles.
  • Path planning: Selecting a suitable route towards the destination.
  • Obstacle detection and avoidance: Recognising an obstruction and changing movement when required.

These functions may use different sources of information. A robot travelling through a building can estimate movement using wheel encoders and motion sensors, while cameras or distance sensors help it detect nearby objects.

Satellite navigation and local sensing

Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) provide positioning information using signals from navigation satellites. The United States' Global Positioning System (GPS) is one such system. India's Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) is an independent regional satellite-navigation system.

According to ISRO's information published on 24 January 2025, NavIC is designed to serve India and an area extending approximately 1,500 km beyond the Indian landmass as its primary service area. ISRO identifies 2 service categories: Standard Positioning Service (SPS) for general users and Restricted Service (RS) for authorised users.

A satellite-navigation receiver can help determine outdoor location, but it does not directly reveal whether a chair, person or wall is immediately ahead of a robot. Local obstacle detection generally requires other sensors. Satellite positioning can also be unsuitable or unavailable in certain indoor and obstructed environments.

Other aids to navigation

MethodInformation providedImportant limitation
GNSS receiverPosition from satellite signalsSignal reception may be poor indoors or near obstructions
Magnetic compassDirection relative to the magnetic fieldDoes not determine the robot's exact location
Wheel encoderWheel rotation used to estimate movementWheel slipping can introduce error
CameraVisual features of the surroundingsPerformance depends on conditions and processing
LiDAR or ultrasonic sensorDistances to surrounding objectsDoes not independently provide a complete route decision

A magnetic compass works because a freely moving magnet tends to align along the north-south direction. The compass therefore helps determine direction, but a direction reading and a position estimate are different pieces of information.

Example: a warehouse delivery robot

Suppose a robot must take a package from storage to a collection point. It estimates its location, selects a route and begins moving. If a trolley blocks the route, its sensors detect the obstruction. The controller may stop the robot or select another permitted route. The robot then continues towards its destination when conditions allow.

Such navigation can be performed using information processed locally. Continuous Internet access is not a necessary condition for a robot to avoid an obstacle.

Prelims focus

  • Localisation means estimating present position; path planning means selecting a route.
  • GNSS provides satellite-based positioning information.
  • GPS is associated with the United States; NavIC is India's regional navigation system.
  • NavIC's primary service area covers India and about 1,500 km beyond the Indian landmass.
  • NavIC offers SPS and RS.
  • Trap: Satellite navigation alone is not a substitute for nearby obstacle detection.

[Sources: ISRO, NVS-02: Advancing India's Regional Navigation Capabilities, 24 January 2025, sections on NavIC coverage and services, accessed 2026-11-05; ISRO, IRNSS Programme, overview and applications, accessed 2026-11-05; NCERT, Curiosity, Class 6, Exploring Magnets, section 4.3, printed pp.65–66, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volume 28; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Motion, section 8.1, consulted in GPSC textbook compendium volume 31.]
